title: Multi-head Latent Attention: caching one small vector instead of all K and V
body:
**The problem with regular MHA.** At inference, each token's keys and values must be kept for every later token. For one layer you store $2 \cdot n_h d_h$ numbers per token ($n_h$ heads $\times$ head dim $d_h$, times 2 for K and V). With $n_h d_h = d_{\text{model}}$, that is $2 d_{\text{model}}$ numbers per token per layer — the cache grows linearly with context length and dominates memory at long context.

**MLA's idea: cache a compressed latent.** Instead of projecting $h_t$ straight to K and V, DeepSeek-V3 first projects it **down** to a small latent vector
$$c_t^{KV} = W^{DKV} h_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_c},\qquad d_c \ll n_h d_h$$
and then **up** again at use time: $K = W^{UK} c_t^{KV}$, $V = W^{UV} c_t^{KV}$. Only $c_t^{KV}$ is cached. In DeepSeek-V3, $d_c = 512$ while $n_h d_h = 128 \times 128 = 16384$, so $2 d_{\text{model}}$-sized storage collapses to roughly $d_c$ plus a small shared RoPE key.

**Why it isn't just "MHA with fewer dims".** The up-projections $W^{UK}, W^{UV}$ are fixed matrices, so they can be **absorbed** into $W^Q$ and the output projection $W^O$ at inference. No K or V is ever materialised per head; the latent is attended to directly. Expressive power stays near full MHA because each head still gets its own up-projection, unlike GQA/MQA which make heads *share* one K/V.

**The RoPE wrinkle.** Rotary embeddings are position-dependent, so they can't be absorbed into a static matrix. MLA therefore splits keys: a compressed part from $c_t^{KV}$, plus a small *decoupled* RoPE key $k_t^R$ (64 dims in V3) shared across heads. The cache holds $d_c + d_h^R = 512 + 64 = 576$ numbers per token per layer.

**Net effect:** per-token cache drops from $\sim$16k–32k values to 576 — an order-of-magnitude cut — with quality reported comparable to or better than full MHA.

more.label: Compare with MQA and GQA
more.text:
All three shrink the KV cache, but differently.

• MQA: all heads share ONE key head and ONE value head. Cache = 2*d_h per token. Cheapest, but heads lose independent key/value subspaces, and quality typically drops.

• GQA: heads are split into g groups sharing K/V. Cache = 2*g*d_h. A tunable middle ground (Llama-family uses this).

• MLA: every head keeps its own up-projection W^UK, W^UV, so heads are not forced to share a subspace — the sharing is a low-rank bottleneck instead. Cache = d_c + d_h^R.

Intuition: MQA/GQA cut the number of heads you store; MLA cuts the *rank* of what you store.

more.label: Worked number (DeepSeek-V3 config)
more.text:
Config: 61 layers, n_h = 128 heads, d_h = 128, d_c = 512, decoupled RoPE key dim = 64.

If V3 used plain MHA, per token per layer:
2 * 128 * 128 = 32,768 values.

With MLA:
512 + 64 = 576 values.

Ratio ≈ 32768 / 576 ≈ 57x smaller per layer.

For a 100,000-token context in bf16 (2 bytes), all 61 layers:
• MHA-equivalent: 32,768 * 2 * 61 * 100,000 ≈ 400 GB
• MLA: 576 * 2 * 61 * 100,000 ≈ 7 GB

That is the difference between a context that will not fit on a node and one that will. (Numbers follow from the published config; treat them as the arithmetic, not a benchmark.)

more.label: Common misconception
more.text:
"MLA saves memory because the model is smaller / uses fewer parameters."

No — MLA actually ADDS parameters (the down- and up-projection matrices) and adds a little compute. The saving is purely in what must be *stored per token at inference*. Weights are paid for once; the KV cache is paid for once per token, per layer, per sequence in the batch. Trading a few extra static matrices for a 50x smaller per-token cache is a very good deal at long context and large batch — and because the up-projections are absorbed into W^Q and W^O, the extra inference compute is close to zero.
